claims.text: Generalized entropy inequality indices from economics can quantify algorithmic unfairness by measuring the inequality of benefits received by individuals or groups from prediction outcomes.
Overall individual-level unfairness measured by generalized entropy indices can be additively decomposed into a between-group unfairness component and a within-group unfairness component.
Minimizing exclusively the between-group component of algorithmic unfairness can increase within-group unfairness.
Minimizing exclusively the between-group component of algorithmic unfairness can increase overall individual unfairness.
A classifier achieves zero individual unfairness under a zero-normalized inequality index if and only if a classifier achieves zero empirical prediction loss.
The proportional contribution of between-group unfairness to overall individual unfairness increases as sensitive feature groups are refined through intersectionality.

evidence.description: The authors define benefit functions bi = y_hat_i - y_i + 1 for individuals and plug them into generalized entropy indices E_alpha(b1, ..., bn) to quantify individual and group unfairness.
Generalized entropy E_alpha(b) is shown mathematically to decompose into E_alpha_omega(b) (within-group) and E_alpha_beta(b) (between-group) for any disjoint population partition G.

Proposition 3.3 proves that optimizing solely for between-group fairness increases within-group unfairness, and experiments on the COMPAS dataset show within-group unfairness for Whites increases as between-group constraints tighten.
On the COMPAS dataset, reducing between-group unfairness by tightening the covariance multiplicative factor from 0.8 to 0.6 increases the overall individual unfairness E2(b).
Proposition 3.1 proves that for zero-normalized I(.), there exists theta with ID(theta) = 0 if and only if there exists theta' with LD(theta') = 0.

Proposition 3.4 proves between-group inequality over Cartesian product partitions is monotonically non-decreasing, and COMPAS experiments show between-group contribution rises from under 1% for 2 groups to nearly 10% for 18 intersected groups.

methodologies.name: Generalized Entropy Unfairness Measurement Framework
methodologies.description: Quantifies algorithmic unfairness by mapping classifier predictions to individual non-negative benefit functions and evaluating benefit distributions using subgroup-decomposable Generalized Entropy indices.
conditions: support vector machine with RBF kernel

limitations.text: Existing measures of inequality in benefits are limited to handling non-negative benefit values.
Determining exact numerical benefit values for different outcome types depends on context and task and may vary in difficulty in practice.
Prior group fairness definitions do not provide principled quantitative measures for the scalar degree of unfairness when an algorithm is unfair.
Existing group fairness measures fail to consider relative population sizes of different groups when estimating unfairness.

future_work.text: Extend the inequality index-based unfairness measurement framework to unsupervised learning tasks such as clustering and ranking.
